briefs.problem: There is no fast, reliable way to confirm who has actually arrived at the event and let them in, beyond a manual or nonexistent process.
briefs.solution: A staff-facing app to identify arriving attendees (scan or search) and record their entry at the venue.
introduces: an attendee-list sync mechanism from registration into a device-held snapshot
offline-capable check-in with later sync and conflict handling (if connectivity can't be guaranteed)
concurrency handling across multiple simultaneous entrance devices
a check-in data model distinguishing duplicate, re-entry, and zone/session access

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed, not confirmed
challenges.premise: The request describes 'staff scan/check in attendees' as if the app will simply work at the door.
challenges.alternative: Treat offline capability as the default architecture — a local attendee snapshot with sync-on-reconnect — until a venue survey proves constant connectivity, since the cost of assuming connectivity and being wrong is discovered on the event floor with no fix window.
challenges.consequence: If built online-only and the venue wifi or 4G saturates during peak arrival, check-in fails visibly in front of the client with no way to patch it that day.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm connectivity guarantees (or the absence of them) and schedule a venue/network check before locking the architecture.

challenges.headline: Check-in treated as a boolean
challenges.premise: The request implies a single scan = single check-in, with no stated handling for a second scan of the same attendee.
challenges.alternative: Model check-in as a logged event carrying zone/session context, so a second scan can be classified as duplicate, re-entry, or a different zone/session access rather than a single flag.
challenges.consequence: A boolean model breaks the moment two doors scan the same attendee within seconds of each other, and it can't represent legitimate re-entry or multi-zone access without a rebuild.
challenges.recommendation: Define the duplicate/re-entry/zone-access rule with the client before the data model is fixed, and decide if it varies by entrance.

challenges.headline: One-off build assumed by default
challenges.premise: The request is scoped as if this is a single-event tool, with no mention of future events.
challenges.alternative: Settle explicitly whether this is a throwaway build or the first instance of a reusable event kit, since that decision shapes the data model (single-event vs multi-event), configurability, and cost before any code is written.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event and discovering later that a second event is wanted forces a retrofit of the data model, branding, and configuration — considerably more expensive than deciding upfront.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether more events are planned before estimating.

complexity_reasons: offline/sync architecture undecided but likely required
briefs.cost_driver: the offline-sync architecture and attendee-list volatility handling, not the scan UI itself
risks: Building assuming reliable connectivity, then discovering the venue can't support it on the day, with no time to redesign.
Defining check-in as a simple flag and having it collapse under concurrent multi-door scanning.
No confirmed source for the attendee list — if it's not a live feed, walk-ins and substitutions will have no on-site path.
Attendee PII (and possibly photos) handled with no stated permissions or GDPR retention plan.
No reporting spec agreed, risking a post-event deliverable that doesn't match what the client (or their sponsors) actually needs.

opportunities.text: If more than one event is likely, build the offline snapshot + sync engine and the attendee/category model as a reusable kit now rather than retrofitting later.
Design the post-event attendance export as a configurable format from the start, since sponsors, invoicing and compliance will each want a different cut of the same check-in data.

next_steps: Confirm with the client whether this is a one-off build or the first event of a reusable kit — this decides the data model before anything else.
Run a venue connectivity check (or get a firm guarantee) before committing to an online-only or offline-first architecture.
Define the check-in rule (duplicate vs re-entry vs zone access) and whether it varies by entrance, with the event manager and on-site staff.
Clarify where the attendee list comes from, how often it updates, and what happens for walk-ins and substitutions on the day.

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed, not confirmed
challenges.premise: The request describes staff scanning attendees as if the device will simply be online at the venue.
challenges.alternative: Treating offline capability as a default architectural requirement — local snapshot of the attendee list plus deferred sync — costs more upfront but avoids a rebuild if the venue's wifi/4G turns out to be unreliable, which is the norm rather than the exception for this kind of app.
challenges.consequence: If the app is built online-only and connectivity fails on the day, there is no fallback and no second chance — the failure happens live in front of the client at the door.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm the offline requirement with the client before architecture is fixed, and treat it as a default rather than a stretch feature.

challenges.headline: Check-in treated as a boolean
challenges.premise: The request implies a single scan action: attendee arrives, gets checked in.
challenges.alternative: Modeling check-in as an event log per attendee — distinguishing duplicate, re-entry, and zone/session access — supports the real cases (someone stepping out and back in, access to a second session) without needing a rebuild later.
challenges.consequence: A boolean check-in model will mishandle re-entries and multi-zone attendees, forcing a data-model change once the first real event exposes the gap.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify with the client what a second scan of the same attendee should mean before designing the data model.

challenges.headline: One-off build vs reusable kit

challenges.alternative: Scoping the attendee/category/zone model as multi-event from the start costs little extra now, versus retrofitting a reusable structure once a second event is requested.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event-only now and needing a second event later means re-architecting the data model, configuration and admin surface rather than reusing them.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether more events are planned before locking the data model.
